verses.verse:
आद्या जिह्वाती तत्र सुवाधा बालकैरपि।
उच्छिष्टा गंधयुक्ता ष स्वासनाद नियन्त्रिता।३८।
verses.text: Of these, the first, the Jihvāvatī, is easy to play even for children; [but] it is defiled by the mouth, it carries a smell, and its breath and sound are fixed.

commentary.text: That is, the Jihvāvatī flute is very easy to play; for this quality alone even children like it. But its various [faults] are not seen by everyone. Faults: (1) It is always jūṭhā (defiled by the mouth). So to some extent it is a cause of infectious disease. (2) If it is not washed again and again, it also smells bad, so that one does not feel like playing it. (3) The breath and the nāda (sound) are also fixed. That is, if the flute-maker has made it alpāhārī (taking little breath), that flute can be played only with little breath; if for some reason the player is not in a position to give little breath, he cannot play it. Besides these faults there is a fourth fault as well: in winter, as one goes on playing, water collects in the flute, so that its mouth-hole fills up and its very sound begins to vanish. In this situation the player flicks it like a pen to get the water out of its jihvā (fipple); by this action the flute may break, and a social offence is also possible. In each of the flutes above the condition of the mouth-hole is different, so even though the process of playing is the same, there is a difference in the act of blowing. So now let us attend to the merits and faults of the Kṛṣṇā, that is the āḍī bansī (transverse flute).

terms.en: Jihvāvatī — flute with a fipple (duct flute)
